SPARK: Representation-Level KV Memory Alignment for Safer Vision-Language Models

Mohd Azfar ††thanks: Corresponding author.    Izhar Dad Khan
Abstract

Vision-language models (VLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks that distribute harmful intent across text and images, making unimodal safety mechanisms insufficient. We investigate whether this vulnerability can be mitigated directly in the multimodal key–value (KV) memory formed during prefill, without modifying model parameters at inference time. We introduce SPARK, a two-stage framework for targeted KV-memory repair. Stage 1 uses a disposable diagnostic adapter to identify harm-associated directions in multimodal key and value representations. Stage 2 projects out these directions, learns a lightweight residual repair, and anchors repaired keys with an image-structural prior to preserve visual grounding. Rather than applying the intervention uniformly, SPARK mixes repaired and original memory using a head-wise coefficient gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} determined by intervention-relevant subspace energy EhE_{h}, requiring no explicit harm classifier at inference.

Across LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Chameleon-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B, and InternVL2-4B, SPARK reduces multimodal attack success while preserving general capability. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, image-only jailbreak attack success falls to 4.7%, while MMMU remains within 0.6 points of the undefended model (47.8 vs. 48.4) with near-baseline language quality. On MM-SafetyBench, attack success decreases from 39.2% to 12.4%. Even under white-box adaptive joint prompt–image attacks, attack success is limited to 20.3%, compared with 54.6% for the undefended model. These results suggest that multimodal jailbreak behavior can be substantially mitigated by selectively repairing intervention-relevant KV subspaces at prefill, particularly when harmful evidence is carried by the visual modality.

1 Introduction

Vision-language models (VLMs) now achieve strong multimodal reasoning across benchmarks and applications [9, 26], but multimodal inputs introduce safety failures that language-only alignment does not fully cover. Harmful prompts, adversarial images, and cross-modal jailbreaks can bypass otherwise aligned behavior [22, 12, 11, 25]. Inference-time steering, projection, and activation revision can improve refusal, yet broad edits also suppress representations needed for benign reasoning [22, 12, 10]. The task is to localize the intervention enough to keep useful capability.

An unsafe output does not identify the internal directions of that behavioral shift, and a harmful–benign contrast further mixes the shift with ordinary image and prompt differences. We ask whether safety-relevant displacement can be isolated on a fixed input, localized in the key–value (KV) states that form attention memory, and scaled by how strongly those directions are expressed at inference. This splits three usually coupled problems: what to suppress, how to recover useful information lost by that suppression, and how much each attention head should be edited.

We instantiate this with SPARK. Stage 1 trains a discarded diagnostic adapter on harmful calibration inputs; paired KV residuals against the frozen model on the same inputs yield harm-calibrated displacement subspaces, which are then removed by orthogonal projection. Stage 2 adds restorative KV residuals on the projected cache, with key-side structural grounding, a reconstruction penalty, and query-side separation so the repair does not rebuild the suppressed directions.

Always-on projection would still discard useful information when those directions are weakly expressed. For each head, SPARK measures the energy EhE_{h} of the current KV state in the frozen subspaces and obtains a closed-form mix gh⋆∈[0,1]g_{h}^{\star}\in[0,1] between original and repaired memory. gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} is intervention strength from the KV state, not a learned estimate of P⁡(harmful∣x)P(\mathrm{harmful}\mid x). The edited cache is written once at prefill and reused during generation.

In summary, our contributions are: (1) input-matched KV subspace discovery from a temporary diagnostic perturbation on fixed inputs; (2) a project-and-repair KV intervention with key-side structural grounding and query-side separation; (3) a head-wise closed-form mix gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} from subspace energy EhE_{h}, without a learned harm detector; and (4) an evaluation of safety, utility, robustness, and overhead, with ablations of the subspaces, restorative losses, and the adaptive mix.

2 Related Work

Multimodal safety and inference-time alignment.

Safety alignment inherited from a language backbone can degrade after multimodal adaptation, and adversarial images can interact with text to circumvent aligned behavior [3, 11, 25]. Defenses include safety instruction tuning [3], prompt-level safeguards [24, 28], and inference-time representation interventions [20, 10, 22, 12, 18].

Steering edits safety- or refusal-associated directions; AutoSteer additionally localizes those directions and uses an internal prober to switch the edit on [22, 18]. Internal Activation Revision and head-specific methods likewise target activations [10, 5], and HiddenDetect shows that LVLM hidden states carry jailbreak-predictive signals [8]. SPARK uses this representation-level view but edits attention memory: how KK and VV move under a controlled shift toward harmful completion, written once at prefill rather than steered in the residual stream at decode.

Safety subspaces and behavioral displacement.

Low-dimensional directions have been linked to safety and refusal. VLM-Guard estimates them from representation contrasts and projects them out [12]; InferAligner similarly uses internal states at inference [20]. A harmful–benign contrast, however, changes both the input and the behavior, so the residual also contains ordinary image and prompt variation. SPARK instead measures an input-matched displacement. For a fixed harmful calibration input xhx_{h}, a temporary Diagnostic Stress Adapter (DSA) induces a controlled safety-degrading perturbation,

Δ​X​(xh)=XDSA​(xh)−Xbase​(xh).\Delta X(x_{h})=X^{\mathrm{DSA}}(x_{h})-X^{\mathrm{base}}(x_{h}). (1)

Holding the input fixed isolates the change due to that diagnostic shift. SPARK estimates it separately for keys and values and takes the dominant activation-space directions as the bases later edited.

Fact editing and KV-cache compression.

Transformer attention is

Attn⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤d)​V,\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V, (2)

with keys shaping addressing and values carrying retrieved content [17, 6]. Earlier methods used related memory pathways to edit factual associations (ROME, MEMIT) and to compress the attention cache at test time (H2O, Scissorhands) [15, 16, 27, 14]. SPARK is neither: it edits the attention KV cache for multimodal safety, projecting harm-calibrated KK/VV directions, restoring useful structure, and mixing original vs. repaired memory with a head-wise coefficient from the current KV state.

3 Method

3.1 Overview

SPARK decomposes KV-space safety intervention into two stages (Figure 1). Stage 1 uses a temporary harmful adaptation as a diagnostic probe and measures the resulting displacement of key and value activations relative to the frozen base model. Dominant directions of these input-matched residuals define harm-calibrated KV displacement subspaces, which are removed through orthogonal projection. Stage 2 operates on the projected cache and learns lightweight restorative residuals that recover useful information removed by the projection while discouraging reconstruction of the suppressed subspaces. At inference, a head-wise coefficient gh⋆​(x)∈[0,1]g_{h}^{\star}(x)\in[0,1] interpolates between the original and projected-and-repaired KV representations. The prefill KV cache is the persistent representation through which multimodal evidence conditions subsequent autoregressive decoding; SPARK therefore intervenes once after multimodal prefill so the repaired memory persists for the full generation without repeated decode-time steering.

Let fθf_{\theta} denote the frozen VLM and x=(xv,xt)x=(x_{v},x_{t}) an image–text input. At layer ll and attention head hh,

K(l,h)\displaystyle K^{(l,h)} =H(l)​WK(l,h),\displaystyle=H^{(l)}W_{K}^{(l,h)}, (3)
V(l,h)\displaystyle V^{(l,h)} =H(l)​WV(l,h).\displaystyle=H^{(l)}W_{V}^{(l,h)}.

We intervene on a fixed set of layers and heads selected on the validation split; unless ambiguity arises, we suppress the layer index ll for readability.

3.2 Stage 1: harm-calibrated KV displacement discovery

Behavioral supervision identifies whether a model produces an unsafe completion, but does not directly identify the internal directions associated with that behavioral transition. Decomposing raw harmful activations can retain ordinary image and prompt semantics in addition to safety-relevant variation. We therefore estimate an input-matched behavioral displacement.

We freeze fθf_{\theta} and train a rank-rDSAr_{\mathrm{DSA}} Diagnostic Stress Adapter (DSA), Δ​WDSA\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}} [7], on a harmful calibration set 𝒟h\mathcal{D}_{h} to induce a controlled shift toward unsafe completions (supplementary Section S11). For every x∈𝒟hx\in\mathcal{D}_{h} we record key and value activations from the frozen base model and the DSA-perturbed model. For head hh,

Δ​XK(h)\displaystyle\Delta X_{K}^{(h)} =XKDSA,(h)−XKbase,(h),\displaystyle=X_{K}^{\mathrm{DSA},(h)}-X_{K}^{\mathrm{base},(h)}, (4)
Δ​XV(h)\displaystyle\Delta X_{V}^{(h)} =XVDSA,(h)−XVbase,(h).\displaystyle=X_{V}^{\mathrm{DSA},(h)}-X_{V}^{\mathrm{base},(h)}.

Δ​WDSA\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}} is the diagnostic perturbation; Δ​XK(h)\Delta X_{K}^{(h)} and Δ​XV(h)\Delta X_{V}^{(h)} measure its realized effect on the activations of the same inputs. After stacking token-level residuals, Δ​XK(h)∈ℝN×dk\Delta X_{K}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{k}} and Δ​XV(h)∈ℝN×dv\Delta X_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{v}}. Independent SVDs

Δ​XK(h)\displaystyle\Delta X_{K}^{(h)} =𝒰K(h)​ΣK(h)​PK(h)⊤,\displaystyle=\mathcal{U}_{K}^{(h)}\Sigma_{K}^{(h)}P_{K}^{(h)\top}, (5)
Δ​XV(h)\displaystyle\Delta X_{V}^{(h)} =𝒰V(h)​ΣV(h)​PV(h)⊤,\displaystyle=\mathcal{U}_{V}^{(h)}\Sigma_{V}^{(h)}P_{V}^{(h)\top},

retain the leading rsr_{s} right singular vectors PK(h)∈ℝdk×rsP_{K}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times r_{s}} and PV(h)∈ℝdv×rsP_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times r_{s}}, with PK(h)⊤​PK(h)=IP_{K}^{(h)\top}P_{K}^{(h)}=I and PV(h)⊤​PV(h)=IP_{V}^{(h)\top}P_{V}^{(h)}=I. We refer to their spans as the harm-calibrated key and value displacement subspaces.

We decompose the activation residuals rather than Δ​WDSA\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}}. Even under Δ​XK≈H​Δ​WK\Delta X_{K}\approx H\Delta W_{K}, the hidden representation HH varies across tokens, samples, and modalities. Activation-space SVD therefore identifies the directions along which the realized KV states move and places the bases in the spaces subsequently edited.

After subspace extraction, the DSA is discarded and PK(h),PV(h)P_{K}^{(h)},P_{V}^{(h)} are frozen. Independently estimated bases remain substantially overlapping under seed and discovery changes (projection similarity S⁡(Ua,Ub)S(U_{a},U_{b}); supplementary Section S9, Table S22).

Hard KV projection.

The orthogonal projectors are ΠK(h)=PK(h)​PK(h)⊤\Pi_{K}^{(h)}=P_{K}^{(h)}P_{K}^{(h)\top} and ΠV(h)=PV(h)​PV(h)⊤\Pi_{V}^{(h)}=P_{V}^{(h)}P_{V}^{(h)\top}. For each targeted head,

K⟂,(h)\displaystyle K^{\perp,(h)} =K(h)​(I−ΠK(h)),\displaystyle=K^{(h)}\bigl(I-\Pi_{K}^{(h)}\bigr), (6)
V⟂,(h)\displaystyle V^{\perp,(h)} =V(h)​(I−ΠV(h)).\displaystyle=V^{(h)}\bigl(I-\Pi_{V}^{(h)}\bigr).

By construction, K⟂,(h)​PK(h)=0K^{\perp,(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}=0 and V⟂,(h)​PV(h)=0V^{\perp,(h)}P_{V}^{(h)}=0. This projection provides SPARK’s primary mechanism for removing the calibrated displacement components. The extracted directions need not be harm-exclusive: always-on projection lowers ASR and MMMU together (45.9 vs. 47.9 gated; Table 3). Stage 2 learns to repair projection-induced information loss while discouraging reconstruction of the suppressed components.

3.3 Stage 2: restorative KV alignment

To repair that information loss without undoing Stage 1, an independent lightweight adapter with parameters ϕ\phi produces restorative residuals from the model representation, Δ​Kϕ(l,h)=H(l)​Δ​WK,ϕ(l,h)\Delta K_{\phi}^{(l,h)}=H^{(l)}\Delta W_{K,\phi}^{(l,h)} and Δ​Vϕ(l,h)=H(l)​Δ​WV,ϕ(l,h)\Delta V_{\phi}^{(l,h)}=H^{(l)}\Delta W_{V,\phi}^{(l,h)}, which are added to the projected cache:

Ks,(h)\displaystyle K^{s,(h)} =K⟂,(h)+Δ​Kϕ(h),\displaystyle=K^{\perp,(h)}+\Delta K_{\phi}^{(h)}, (7)
Vs,(h)\displaystyle V^{s,(h)} =V⟂,(h)+Δ​Vϕ(h).\displaystyle=V^{\perp,(h)}+\Delta V_{\phi}^{(h)}.

The adapter does not repeat (6); it restores information after projection, subject to the three constraints below.

Structural restoration.

To mitigate collateral loss of visual grounding after projection, we introduce a lightweight structural prior on the repaired keys. Matching KsK^{s} to the model’s own visual features would restore the appearance that produced the completion; we instead instantiate the prior with Canny edges [1], a deterministic, training-free boundary map that keeps layout without adding learned semantics. Canny is a simple structural anchor, not assumed uniquely optimal (Section S18). Passing C⁡(xv)C(x_{v}) through the frozen visual pathway and frozen key projection yields Gedge(l,h)​(xv)∈ℝT×dkG_{\mathrm{edge}}^{(l,h)}(x_{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{k}}. The repaired key branch is constrained by

ℒground=∑h‖Ks,(h)−Gedge(h)​(xv)‖F2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ground}}=\sum_{h}\bigl\|K^{s,(h)}-G_{\mathrm{edge}}^{(h)}(x_{v})\bigr\|_{F}^{2}. (8)

We apply the structural prior only to keys. Keys participate in the attention addressing scores through Q​K⊤QK^{\top}, whereas values carry the content retrieved after those weights are formed. Matching both drops MMMU from 47.9 to 44.5 (Table 3).

Discouraging subspace reconstruction.

The restorative adapter could otherwise reconstruct components eliminated by Stage 1. We penalize energy along the frozen displacement bases:

ℒrecon=∑h(‖Ks,(h)​PK(h)‖F2+‖Vs,(h)​PV(h)‖F2).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}=\sum_{h}\Bigl(\|K^{s,(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}+\|V^{s,(h)}P_{V}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}\Bigr). (9)

Since K⟂,(h)​PK(h)=V⟂,(h)​PV(h)=0K^{\perp,(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}=V^{\perp,(h)}P_{V}^{(h)}=0, this is equivalently energy of the residuals alone, ∑h(‖Δ​Kϕ(h)​PK(h)‖F2+‖Δ​Vϕ(h)​PV(h)‖F2)\sum_{h}\bigl(\|\Delta K_{\phi}^{(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}+\|\Delta V_{\phi}^{(h)}P_{V}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}\bigr). The adapter is thus encouraged to restore information outside, rather than reconstruct information inside, the suppressed subspaces.

Query-side separation.

Queries and keys of each head share the same inner-product space, so PK(l,h)P_{K}^{(l,h)} also identifies query components aligned with the suppressed key directions. SPARK does not edit QQ; it penalizes that alignment:

ℒsep=1H​∑h=1H‖Q(h)​PK(h)‖F‖Q(h)‖F+ϵ.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{\|Q^{(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}\|_{F}}{\|Q^{(h)}\|_{F}+\epsilon}. (10)

KV projection removes the calibrated directions from memory; (10) reduces query components along the same key-space directions. Removing this term raises ASR from 5.2 to 9.8 (Table 3; supplementary Section S4).

3.4 Head-wise adaptive intervention

Uniformly replacing the original cache with the projected-and-repaired branch can unnecessarily perturb heads whose current KV state lies mostly outside the Stage 1 bases. SPARK therefore assigns each targeted head an adaptive coefficient. For a generic strength gh∈[0,1]g_{h}\in[0,1],

Kout,(h)\displaystyle K^{\mathrm{out},(h)} =(1−gh)​K(h)+gh​Ks,(h),\displaystyle=(1-g_{h})K^{(h)}+g_{h}K^{s,(h)}, (11)
Vout,(h)\displaystyle V^{\mathrm{out},(h)} =(1−gh)​V(h)+gh​Vs,(h).\displaystyle=(1-g_{h})V^{(h)}+g_{h}V^{s,(h)}.

Thus gh=0g_{h}{=}0 leaves head hh unchanged, gh=1g_{h}{=}1 applies the full projected-and-repaired representation, and intermediate values yield a graded intervention. There is no sample-level or layer-level coefficient. At inference we use the closed form gh=gh⋆g_{h}=g_{h}^{\star} derived below.

Unlike a prompt-level safety detector, gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} is not trained to approximate P⁡(harmful∣x)P(\mathrm{harmful}\mid x). It follows from a trade-off between energy in the Stage 1 bases and the cost of editing the cache. For head hh, the intervention-relevant subspace energy (energy in those bases, not a harmfulness score) is

Eh​(x)=‖K(h)​PK(h)‖F2+‖V(h)​PV(h)‖F2.E_{h}(x)=\|K^{(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}+\|V^{(h)}P_{V}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}. (12)

After mixing, the same quantity on the deployed cache is

ℒres=∑h(‖Kout,(h)​PK(h)‖F2+‖Vout,(h)​PV(h)‖F2),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{res}}=\sum_{h}\Bigl(\|K^{\mathrm{out},(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}+\|V^{\mathrm{out},(h)}P_{V}^{(h)}\|_{F}^{2}\Bigr), (13)

and the cost of editing a head is

ℒint=1B​H​∑i=1B∑h=1Hgh​(xi).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}=\frac{1}{BH}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{h=1}^{H}g_{h}(x_{i}). (14)

Collecting these mix terms with the Stage 2 constraints, the objective with fθf_{\theta} frozen is

ℒSPARK=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPARK}}={} α​ℒres+β​ℒground+γ​ℒrecon\displaystyle\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{res}}+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ground}}+\gamma\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}} (15)
+δ​ℒsep+λ​ℒint.\displaystyle+\delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}.

ℒres\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{res}} rewards suppression of intervention-relevant KV components; ℒint\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}} charges for modifying a head. This yields a per-head minimum-intervention rule.

Optimal intervention strength.

If the repaired branch already lies outside the Stage 1 bases, Ks,(h)​PK(h)=Vs,(h)​PV(h)=0K^{s,(h)}P_{K}^{(h)}=V^{s,(h)}P_{V}^{(h)}=0 (the target of ℒrecon\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}; supplementary Section S2), mixing leaves only a (1−gh)(1-g_{h}) fraction of the original subspace energy. The ghg_{h}-dependent part of (15) then separates per head as

𝒥h​(gh)=α​(1−gh)2​Eh​(x)+λ​gh,gh∈[0,1].\mathcal{J}_{h}(g_{h})=\alpha(1-g_{h})^{2}E_{h}(x)+\lambda g_{h},\qquad g_{h}\in[0,1]. (16)

The first term shrinks residual energy as ghg_{h} grows; the second charges for editing. 𝒥h\mathcal{J}_{h} is convex, and for Eh​(x)>0E_{h}(x)>0 unconstrained stationarity is

d2​𝒥hd​gh2\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}\mathcal{J}_{h}}{dg_{h}^{2}} =2​α​Eh​(x)≥0,\displaystyle=2\alpha E_{h}(x)\geq 0, (17)
1−gh\displaystyle 1-g_{h} =λ2​α​Eh​(x).\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda}{2\alpha E_{h}(x)}.

Clipping that critical point to [0,1][0,1] yields the unique minimizer

gh⋆​(x)=[1−λ2​α​Eh​(x)][0,1],g_{h}^{\star}(x)=\Bigl[1-\tfrac{\lambda}{2\alpha E_{h}(x)}\Bigr]_{[0,1]}, (18)

where [z][0,1]=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,z}}[z]_{[0,1]}=\min\{1,\max\{0,z\}\}. When Eh​(x)=0E_{h}(x)=0, 𝒥h=λ​gh\mathcal{J}_{h}=\lambda g_{h} and gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}=0. Equivalently, no edit is applied below a threshold on energy:

gh⋆(x)=0⟺Eh(x)≤λ2​α.g_{h}^{\star}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E_{h}(x)\leq\frac{\lambda}{2\alpha}. (19)

Above this cutoff, gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} rises with Eh​(x)E_{h}(x) and approaches one. Thus (16) yields a minimum-cost mix from the current KV-state energy, not a probability that the input is harmful.

We calibrate λ\lambda on a held-out benign pool 𝒟b\mathcal{D}_{b} (n=3,000n{=}3{,}000), disjoint from Stages 1–2 and from MMMU/RWQA, by setting the implicit intervention threshold λ/(2​α)\lambda/(2\alpha) to the 90th percentile of benign per-head intervention-relevant subspace energy EhE_{h}. This is percentile calibration, not optimization of a learned parameter. Under this rule, gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}=0 on 90% of benign (example, head) pairs. Because one input contains many targeted heads, approximately 86% of benign inputs receive no intervention across all targeted heads; equivalently, 14% contain at least one head with gh⋆>0g_{h}^{\star}>0 (Section 4; supplementary Section S5). We report that 14% as an input-level intervention rate, not as the false-positive rate of a harm classifier.

Prefill is then: compute Eh​(x)E_{h}(x) as in (12), set gh⋆​(x)g_{h}^{\star}(x) by (18), and write (11) with gh=gh⋆g_{h}=g_{h}^{\star}. The path is EhE_{h} →\to intervention necessity →\to gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} →\to graded KV correction. There is no binary indicator, no raw-norm statistic, and no learned detector.

4 Experiments

We use LLaVA-OneVision-7B as the primary backbone and report full defense comparisons on Chameleon-7B [2] (Table 2); we additionally test transfer on Qwen2-VL-7B [19] and InternVL2-4B [4] (supplementary Section S10, Table S23). Unless stated, interventions target late vision-heavy layers (18–24), where we observe the clearest activation-hijack patterns in our diagnostics.

4.1 Datasets and Baselines

Data divisions and calibration.

To avoid leakage, we use four disjoint splits: discovery (1k harmful VLSafe examples for subspace extraction), alignment (3k safe/unsafe contrastive pairs with matched prompts for Stage 2), coefficient calibration (3k benign multimodal VQA prompts for the EhE_{h} percentile that sets λ/(2​α)\lambda/(2\alpha), separate from MMMU/RWQA test IDs), and held-out evaluation on unseen safety and capability tests. Alignment pairs pair MS-COCO safe images with matched ToViLaG adversarial contexts to isolate visual hijacking; harmful categories span violence, illegal acts, self-harm, and explicit content. Stage 1 uses unfiltered response activation traces rather than static refusal labels.

Benchmarks and judging metrics.

We report attack success rate (ASR) on VLSafe [3] and on ToViLaG [21] using three evaluation partitions—text, image, and text+image—that we construct for VQA-style jailbreak testing (n=500n{=}500 each; the original ToViLaG paper is a generative toxicity dataset and does not define these partitions), with additional results on MM-SafetyBench in supplementary Section S17 [13]. Capability is measured with MMMU [26] and RealWorldQA [23] (n=500n{=}500 each), together with a cross-modal stress set (noise, near-white, and cropped attacks). Harmfulness uses an instruction-tuned LLM judge with a fixed binary rubric11 1 Three criteria, tie-break rules, and full prompt: supplementary Section S7.; audited agreement is strong (κhuman-human=0.89\kappa_{\text{human-human}}{=}0.89, κLLM-human=0.84\kappa_{\text{LLM-human}}{=}0.84, n=500n{=}500).

Baselines.

Baselines are the undefended LLaVA model [9], Safety SFT [3], Steer/AutoSteer [22] (decode-time hidden-state steering), VLM-Guard [12], OmniSteer [18], and Projection-AlwaysOn (SPARK with gh⋆=1g_{h}^{\star}{=}1 on every targeted head). Table 2 gives matched-protocol reproductions under shared decoding; filtering-only controls are in supplementary Section S8. We focus on memory-level KV editing rather than hybrid input filters, although both can be combined in deployment. For Chameleon Safety SFT we run a fixed-seed sweep over learning rate, warmup, epochs, and weight decay, selecting checkpoints by held-out safety–utility (supplementary Section S15), so the 14.8 MMMU result is not from a single brittle setting.

4.2 Implementation Details

Stage 1 trains a diagnostic stress adapter (rDSA=16r_{\mathrm{DSA}}{=}16) on 1K harmful VLSafe discovery examples only (supplementary Sections S9 and S11; discovery-source ablation Table S21; subspace similarity S⁡(Ua,Ub)S(U_{a},U_{b}) in Table S22). At layers 18–24 we stack per-head key/value activation residuals and take the top rs=8r_{s}{=}8 right singular vectors as bases PK(h),PV(h)P_{K}^{(h)},P_{V}^{(h)} with projectors ΠK(h)=PK(h)​PK(h)⊤\Pi_{K}^{(h)}=P_{K}^{(h)}P_{K}^{(h)\top}; the DSA is then discarded. Stage 2 trains the KV adapter on 3K contrastive pairs. Residual weights on (ℒrecon,ℒground,ℒsep)(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}},\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ground}},\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}) are (1.0,0.6,0.4)(1.0,0.6,0.4). We calibrate λ\lambda on the benign pool by setting λ/(2​α)\lambda/(2\alpha) to the 90th percentile of per-head EhE_{h} (supplementary Section S5); this yields gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}{=}0 on 90% of benign heads and no intervention on ≈86%{\approx}86\% of benign inputs. Optimizer: AdamW, learning rate 2​e−42e^{-4}, batch size 32, 3 epochs, backbone frozen. Harmful validation traces are used only for intervention-rate checks, not for MMMU/RWQA scoring. Prefill uses (11) with gh=gh⋆g_{h}=g_{h}^{\star} from (18). Canny-threshold sensitivity in the main setup is summarized in Table 1. All evaluations are run on 8×\timesA100-80GB GPUs over fixed seeds {13,17,23}\{13,17,23\}. Subspace discovery takes ∼\sim2.1 GPU-hours; training ∼\sim3.4 GPU-hours. Statistical significance is validated via paired bootstrap (p<0.01p<0.01).

4.3 Results

Table 2 reports matched-protocol ASR and capability (MMMU, RealWorldQA) on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Chameleon-7B. On LLaVA-OV, SPARK has the lowest ASR on ToViLaG image-only (4.7%, ‡; next-best 6.8–7.3%) with near-base MMMU/RWQA (47.8/48.4; 60.7/61.8). Steer is lower on VLSafe text (2.0 vs. 3.1), ToViLaG text (1.6 vs. 2.4), and text+image (1.2 vs. 7.4), consistent with language-dominant jailbreaks and decode-time hidden-state steering. On Chameleon, SPARK wins VLSafe text (10.2%, ‡), ToViLaG text (11.9%, ‡), and text+image (9.1 vs. Steer 9.4, ‡), and has the best defense MMMU (31.2 vs. 27.2 VLM-Guard). On Chameleon image-only, Steer is lower (29.3 vs. 31.4) although SPARK remains below OmniSteer (40.8%) and VLM-Guard (37.9%). The 4.7% vs. 31.4% LLaVA–Chameleon image gap reflects early fusion and conservative gating; forcing projection on Chameleon image-only harmful queries lowers ASR to 26.7%26.7\% but increases benign refusals and reduces MMMU (supplementary Section S14, Table S25).

Subspace construction.

Figure 3(a)–(b) support retaining rs=8r_{s}{=}8. Panel (c): input-matched Δ​X\Delta X reaches 5.2 ASR and 47.9 MMMU, versus a harmful–benign contrast (18.0/47.6), SVD of Δ​WDSA\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}} (23.5/47.5), random bases (30.4/47.2), and a benign-VQA subspace (34.6/47.4) (supplementary Sections S5 and S16). Seed/discovery stability of the extracted bases is reported via S⁡(Ua,Ub)S(U_{a},U_{b}) in Section S9 (Table S22).

Head-wise mix.

Figure 3(a)–(c) show overlapping EhE_{h}: most heads sit below T=λ/(2​α)T=\lambda/(2\alpha) (6.2 on the natural-image pool), with a heavier harmful tail rather than a split at Eh=TE_{h}=T. Panel (d) is gh⋆=[1−T/Eh][0,1]g_{h}^{\star}=[1-T/E_{h}]_{[0,1]}; heads with Eh≤TE_{h}\leq T keep gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}=0. Panel (e): at the 90th percentile, 14% of benign inputs and 80% of harmful inputs have at least one head with gh⋆>0g_{h}^{\star}>0 (supplementary Section S5). A lower cutoff raises benign output refusals (9.4% at the 80th row); the 95th percentile leaks unsafe context (11.5% harmful-validation ASR vs. 5.2% at 90th). False triggers concentrate on structurally dense diagrams with naturally high EhE_{h}; forcing gh⋆=1g_{h}^{\star}{=}1 on every head drops AI2D accuracy from 62.4% to 31.2% (selective gh⋆g_{h}^{\star}: 62.0%; supplementary Section S14).

Additional backbones.

We apply the same SPARK protocol (per-backbone EhE_{h} percentile and layer calibration) to Qwen2-VL-7B and InternVL2-4B without reproducing full Steer/OmniSteer grids on those models. SPARK lowers ASR on both: on Qwen2-VL, VLSafe text 45.2%→\rightarrow9.8% and ToViLaG image 58.4%→\rightarrow14.2%, with MMMU 49.1 vs. base 50.3 and RWQA 55.6 vs. 56.8; on InternVL2-4B, VLSafe text 48.7%→\rightarrow12.7% and ToViLaG image 62.1%→\rightarrow17.6%, with MMMU 44.2 vs. 45.8 and RWQA 50.9 vs. 52.4 (supplementary Table S23). Utility drops are small but non-uniform across architectures, consistent with partial rather than identical transfer.

Community and adaptive benchmarks.

We evaluate MM-SafetyBench [13] under the same LLM judge and decoding settings as Table 2 (supplementary Section S17). SPARK ASR is 12.4% versus 39.2% for the base model and below reproduced OmniSteer (14.8%). Under white-box adaptive attacks that target gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} (supplementary Section S17, Table S32), SPARK ASR increases to 15.9–20.3% (joint: 20.3%; AutoSteer 22.7% under the same protocol) and mix bypass (gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}{=}0 on every targeted head) reaches 38.6%, indicating limited robustness to adaptive evasion.

Safety SFT.

Safety SFT [3] is architecture-sensitive in our runs: on Chameleon, the best-of-sweep checkpoint reaches only 14.8 MMMU (supplementary Section S15), while SPARK holds 31.2 with lower ASR on several splits. On LLaVA-OV, Safety SFT is more stable (Table 2). We therefore treat SPARK as a complementary inference-time layer rather than a replacement for training-time alignment.

Ablations.

Ablations (Table 3) support the role of each component. Removing ℒground\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ground}} sharply hurts utility (47.9 →\rightarrow 42.1 MMMU), so the repair needs a structural prior rather than projection alone. Applying ℒground\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ground}} to both Keys and Values also degrades utility (47.9 →\rightarrow 44.5 MMMU), consistent with values carrying content poorly captured by an edge-based structural target, whereas key-only structural grounding preserves downstream reasoning. Removing ℒsep\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}} increases ASR (5.2 →\rightarrow 9.8). Measured on RealWorldQA, ℒsep\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}} leaves the Benign Refusal Rate statistically unchanged (1.2% vs 1.3%), isolating adversarial intent without false triggers on factual sensitive queries. Always-on projection degrades utility (45.9 MMMU), justifying the gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} mix.

Robustness and efficiency.

Under cross-modal stress (supplementary Section S3, Table S3), SPARK shows the largest relative ASR reductions on cropped attacks with localized harmful visual evidence. SPARK adds modest prefill cost (+1.6%) and no per-token decode overhead (supplementary Section S7, Table S18). Relative to AutoSteer (+7.8% decode overhead per token), SPARK’s prefill-once design has lower cumulative cost as generation length grows; OmniSteer and VLM-Guard are not uniformly slower. Figure 5 shows end-to-end scaling (supplementary Section S15).

4.4 Further Analysis

Diagnostics.

Patch/restore and representation checks (supplementary Sections S6 and S13) support intervention-relevant directions, not a single causal mechanism (Table 4; full grid in supplementary Section S6).

Qualitative examples (typography jailbreak, educational blending, and a benign museum query) are in supplementary Figure S1 (Section S20).

Sensitivity analyses.

Layer sweeps: mid layers (12–16) are weaker, deep-only (24–28) under-corrects, and 18–24 is the best balance. Table 1: Canny thresholds barely move RWQA; removing the prior costs 3.8 White-ASR and 5.8 MMMU (Section S8, Table S19). Section S18: shuffled edges hurt more than no prior, while Sobel/HED/blurred Canny stay near default—so the gain is spatial correspondence, not Canny uniquely; input blur/CLIP remain below SPARK (Tables S20, S29, and S36).

5 Conclusion

SPARK estimates harm-calibrated KV directions from a discarded probe, projects them out, restores keys from image structure, and mixes the original cache with head-wise gh⋆g_{h}^{\star}. It improves safety–utility on several visual and cross-modal splits, with lower gains on text-centric jailbreaks and adaptive mix attacks.

Limitations and Ethical Considerations

We evaluate template jailbreaks, stress corruptions, and white-box adaptive attacks (supplementary Section S17). Subspaces use 1k VLSafe examples; permissive EhE_{h} percentiles or OOD attacks can leak unsafe outputs (Section S5). SPARK does not require Canny specifically; we use it as a deterministic, training-free structural prior, and learned or task-adaptive grounding may be stronger. SPARK is not a substitute for safety checks and adversarial testing.

S3 Full Variance Summaries for Reproduced Results

All SPARK and matched-baseline numbers are reported over 3 fixed seeds (13, 17, 23) with mean±\pmstd when shown. MM-SafetyBench, adaptive, and diagnostic extensions use the same LLM judge, decoding settings, and seed set as the main comparison (Table S2). ToViLaG text / image / text+image rows are our VQA-style evaluation partitions of ToViLaG, not an official extra release of that dataset.

S4 Expanded Ablation Variance

Intent separation (ℒs​e​p\mathcal{L}_{sep}, ρ=0\rho{=}0).

ℒs​e​p\mathcal{L}_{sep} penalizes normalized projection of QhQ_{h} onto PKP_{K} with zero margin ρ=0\rho{=}0 during Stage 2 (soft hinge on QQ; adapter residual plus hard projection on K,VK,V at inference, mixed with gh⋆g_{h}^{\star}). Removing ℒs​e​p\mathcal{L}_{sep} raises ASR from 5.2%5.2\% to 9.8%9.8\% (Table S4). Table S5 sweeps ρ\rho under the same Stage 2/gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} protocol; larger ρ\rho relaxes the hinge and increases harmful-val ASR while slightly raising benign refusals.

S5 Rank Stability and Layer/Threshold Sweeps

Calibration of λ\lambda via EhE_{h}.

For each backbone we calibrate λ\lambda on a held-out benign pool (n=3,000n{=}3{,}000 natural-image multimodal VQA prompts; LLaVA-style neutral instructions), disjoint from Phase-1 discovery, Phase-2 alignment, and official MMMU/RWQA test IDs, by setting

λ2​α=Qp​(Eh,𝒟b),\frac{\lambda}{2\alpha}=Q_{p}(E_{h};\mathcal{D}_{b}),

the pp-th percentile of per-head intervention-relevant subspace energy. The default is p=0.90p{=}0.90. This is percentile calibration, not training of a gate network. Then gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}=0 on a fraction pp of benign (example, head) pairs. An input has many targeted heads, so the fraction of benign inputs with every head at gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}=0 is lower. We call the complementary quantity the input-level intervention rate: the fraction of benign inputs with at least one head satisfying gh⋆>0g_{h}^{\star}>0. Table S9 reports that rate in the benign-intervention column, together with a held-out harmful validation set (VLSafe/ToViLaG val) for the harmful-intervention rate (fraction of harmful inputs with at least one gh⋆>0g_{h}^{\star}>0). At p=0.90p{=}0.90, the input-level intervention rate is 0.14±0.020.14\pm 0.02, so ≈86%{\approx}86\% of benign inputs receive no intervention on any targeted head; benign output refusal is a separate judge-based column. Prefill uses (S1) with gh=gh⋆g_{h}=g_{h}^{\star}. MMMU/RWQA capability scores use official benchmark splits only.

S6 Transport and Causal Controls (Variance)

Intervention evidence (not a single-mechanism proof).

Patch/restore and key-resample results in this section and Section S13 test whether identified subspaces causally affect unsafe behavior under our protocol: removing the identified harm-calibrated basis drops ASR to 11.3%11.3\% versus 33.8%33.8\% for a random control, and restore re-inflates compliance. These interventions are supportive of intervention-relevant directions, not a proof that span⁡(PK,PV)\mathrm{span}(P_{K},P_{V}) is an exclusive harmful subspace or that visual hijacking is the only failure mode.

S8 Canny Structural Anchor Robustness

To evaluate whether the geometric preservation provided by the Canny edge anchor is sensitive to hyperparameters, we conducted ablation sweeps over the edge-detection thresholds. The baseline SPARK utilizes standard OpenCV Canny detection with Gaussian blur (σ=1.0\sigma=1.0), a lower hysteresis threshold Tl​o​w=100T_{low}=100, and an upper threshold Th​i​g​h=200T_{high}=200. As in the main paper, the edge map is passed through the frozen visual pathway and the corresponding frozen key projection to obtain Gedge(h)∈ℝT×dkG_{\mathrm{edge}}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{k}}.

Structural anchor scope.

Canny is a fixed nonsemantic key-side regularizer (not a claim that edge detection theoretically removes toxic semantics). Threshold ablations and input-filter comparisons are in Tables S19–S20; edge swaps, key–structure alignment probes, and typography controls are in Section S18.

Lightweight filtering-only control.

To contextualize scope, we additionally evaluate a simple input-filter baseline that applies Gaussian blur (σ=1.0\sigma=1.0) directly to images without KV editing. This control is included to show that lightweight preprocessing can be complementary, but does not match the safety–utility balance of targeted memory intervention.

Canny vs. input filtering.

Three existing controls separate key-side structural anchoring from generic input regularization. Removing the Canny anchor while keeping ℒrecon\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}} and ℒs​e​p\mathcal{L}_{sep} (Table S19) raises stress White-ASR from 8.9%8.9\% to 12.7%12.7\% and drops MMMU from 47.947.9 to 42.142.1, showing that geometry-aware grounding is not redundant with harm-calibrated projection alone. Gaussian blur at the input (Table S20) yields 37.6%37.6\% VLSafe ASR—much weaker than default SPARK (5.2%5.2\%) at similar RWQA (60.060.0 vs. 60.760.7). A stronger CLIP-score safety filter (Section S16, Table S29) improves over blur (24.8%24.8\% ASR) but still sits far above memory-level SPARK with lower MMMU (46.546.5 vs. 47.947.9). Together, these rows argue that SPARK’s gain is not explained by “any” edge map or input scrubbing; it couples harm-calibrated KV editing with a lightweight structural key anchor.

S9 DSA Calibration Diversity and Extraction Reproducibility

Phase-1 calibration scope.

Phase 1 uses n=1,000n{=}1{,}000 harmful VLSafe discovery examples as an operational probe; Phase 2 uses n=3,000n{=}3{,}000 contrastive pairs (disjoint IDs). We do not claim a dataset-agnostic harmful subspace. Supporting evidence: harm-calibrated vs. random/benign displacement subspaces (Table S30), patch/restore (Sections S6, S13), held-out tests and MM-SafetyBench (Section S17), and backbone transfer (Table S23). Table S21 tests whether (PK,PV)(P_{K},P_{V}) depend on a single VLSafe template.

Category stratification (VLSafe discovery).

The 1,000 discovery examples are balanced across:

  • •

    Violence and Physical Harm: 250 examples (25%)

  • •

    Explicit and Adult Content: 250 examples (25%)

  • •

    Illegal Acts and Crime: 250 examples (25%)

  • •

    Self-Harm and Harassment: 250 examples (25%)

While our responsible-use protocol restricts release of tuned DSA weights, we ensure full methodological reproducibility. We will publicly release the exact hashed data indices (from VLSafe/ToViLaG), the deterministic LoRA training scripts, and the downstream SVD extraction module. This allows researchers to independently reconstruct the exact structural subspaces (PK,PVP_{K},P_{V}) without necessitating the release of a reusable malicious generation artifact.

Discovery-source ablation (protocol).

Extract (PK,PV)(P_{K},P_{V}) from three disjoint 1k harmful discovery pools under identical DSA/SVD settings (r=16r{=}16, layers 18–24, top-k=8k{=}8): (A) VLSafe only (main default), (B) ToViLaG harmful only, (C) 500 VLSafe + 500 ToViLaG (matched category quotas). For each (PK,PV)(P_{K},P_{V}), rerun Stage 2 and EhE_{h} percentile calibration with the same seeds and evaluate on held-out ToViLaG (T+I) and official MMMU/RWQA (no test leakage into discovery). Row (A) should reproduce main-paper LLaVA-OV numbers within run variance; close rows across (A–C) would indicate the probe is not a single-source artifact (this does not imply universal generalization).

Stage 1 subspace stability (projection similarity).

A potential concern is that the Stage 1 bases may reflect a particular random seed or discovery set rather than reproducible intervention-relevant structure. We therefore estimate the Stage 1 subspace independently under different discovery conditions and measure the overlap between the resulting bases.

Let Ua,Ub∈ℝd×rU_{a},U_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} denote two independently estimated orthonormal bases. We measure their overlap using mean squared projection similarity,

S⁡(Ua,Ub)=1r​‖Ua⊤​Ub‖F2,S(U_{a},U_{b})=\frac{1}{r}\left\|U_{a}^{\top}U_{b}\right\|_{F}^{2}, (S4)

which equals 11 for identical subspaces and 00 for orthogonal subspaces, and corresponds to the mean squared cosine of their principal angles. Table S22 reports S⁡(Ua,Ub)S(U_{a},U_{b}) under these conditions.

As shown in Table S22, the independently estimated bases retain substantial overlap, with the strongest agreement across random seeds and progressively lower, but still substantial, agreement across disjoint discovery and attack subsets. Together with the consistent downstream safety–utility behavior in Table S21, these results indicate that Stage 1 recovers reproducible intervention-relevant structure rather than an arbitrary seed-specific orientation. Moreover, the substantially weaker protection obtained with a rank-matched random basis (Table S11) shows that arbitrary subspace removal is insufficient to reproduce the effect.

S10 Extended VLM Architectural Generalization

To evaluate the model-agnostic generalizability of SPARK across different visual token-fusion and rotary embedding designs, we extend our evaluation to two additional modern VLM backbones: Qwen2-VL-7B (2D spatial Rotary Position Embeddings and patch-merging) and InternVL2-4B (pixel-shuffle visual-token matching). The results in Table S23 suggest partial transfer with architecture-dependent trade-offs: ASR reductions are meaningful on both backbones, but utility drops and residual ASR differ non-uniformly. For each backbone, EhE_{h} percentiles and layer selections are independently calibrated on held-out validation splits while retaining the same overall SPARK protocol.

S11 Diagnostic Stress Adapter (Stage 1) Training Details

Stage 1 trains a low-rank diagnostic stress adapter (DSA) used only for subspace extraction, not for deployment. The DSA is optimized on harmful calibration completions to amplify measurable activation shifts under unsafe inputs.

Objective and operational extraction.

Let y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) denote token targets from harmful calibration trajectories. We optimize:

ℒDSA\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSA}} =−∑t=1TlogP(yt∣y<t,Ximg,\displaystyle=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P\bigl(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},X_{\mathrm{img}}, (S5)
OPENXprompt;W+Δ​WDSA)\displaystyle X_{\mathrm{prompt}};W+\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}}\bigr)

where Δ​WDSA=B​A⋅αr\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}}=BA\cdot\frac{\alpha}{r}. DSA is a behavioral probe, not the defense: Δ​WDSA\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}} induces a controlled perturbation; we measure the consequence in activation space,

Δ​XK​(x)=XKDSA​(x)−XKbase​(x)\Delta X_{K}(x)=X_{K}^{\mathrm{DSA}}(x)-X_{K}^{\mathrm{base}}(x)

(and likewise for VV), stack tokens/examples per head into RK(h),RV(h)R_{K}^{(h)},R_{V}^{(h)}, and take SVD. PK(h)P_{K}^{(h)} is the leading right-singular basis in ℝdk×rs\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times r_{s}}; the projector is ΠK(h)=PK(h)​PK(h)⊤\Pi_{K}^{(h)}=P_{K}^{(h)}P_{K}^{(h)\top}. We do not SVD Δ​WDSA\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}} (weight space) or raw harmful activations. After extraction, DSA parameters are discarded. Inference applies (S1) on the base model: Ks,(h)=K⟂,(h)+Δ​Kϕ(h)K^{s,(h)}=K^{\perp,(h)}+\Delta K_{\phi}^{(h)} with Δ​Kϕ(h)=H(l)​Δ​WK,ϕ(l,h)\Delta K_{\phi}^{(h)}=H^{(l)}\Delta W_{K,\phi}^{(l,h)} (and likewise VV), mixed with the original cache through ghg_{h}; DSA weights are not released.

Data Details.

The adapter is trained strictly on the 1,000 harmful discovery examples (VLSafe training subset) spanning the four critical categories detailed in Section S9. Matching benign contrastive pairs are excluded from this phase to maximize the representation of target malicious behaviors within the weights.

Hyperparameters.

  • •

    Rank (rDSAr_{\mathrm{DSA}}) and Scaling (α\alpha): rDSA=16r_{\mathrm{DSA}}=16, α=32\alpha=32. Retained SVD rank rs=8r_{s}=8.

  • •

    Target Modules: Key, Value, Query, and Output projection matrices (Wk,Wv,Wq,WoW_{k},W_{v},W_{q},W_{o}) in the self-attention blocks of Layers 18–24.

  • •

    Optimizer & Schedule: AdamW (β1=0.9,β2=0.999\beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999, weight decay =0.01=0.01), learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} with a cosine annealing schedule.

  • •

    Batch Size & Epochs: Batch size of 16 (gradient accumulation =1=1), trained for 3 epochs.

S12 Generation Quality Metrics (Perplexity, Fluency, and Diversity)

To verify that the local key-value safety projection does not introduce language model degradation or repetitive, low-diversity completions, we report three core evaluation sets: perplexity (PPL) measured on WikiText-2, grammatical fluency using the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA) score (MCC ×\times 100), and generation diversity using Distinct-1 and Distinct-2 ratios. Table S24 indicates that SPARK maintains near-identical perplexity, fluency, and vocabulary diversity to the unmodified baseline, with higher Distinct scores than behavioral steering in our runs (which can perturb hidden states and induce repetitive refusal patterns).

S13 Key-Space Path-Patching-Inspired Resample Diagnostic

To provide intervention-level diagnostic detail, we perform a targeted key-space path-patching-inspired resample diagnostic. The objective is to measure the direct intervention effect of deep self-attention key activations (KK) of visual hijack tokens on unsafe completion logits at the model output.

Resampling Ablation Protocol.

Instead of global model intervention, we surgically apply resample ablation strictly to the key activations of visual hijack tokens within the gating-active heads of layers 18–24. Specifically, let Kl,h(i)K_{l,h}^{(i)} represent the key activation of token ii in layer ll and attention head hh. We patch these activations by projecting them onto the complement of the harm-calibrated key basis:

Kl,h(i)​patched\displaystyle K_{l,h}^{(i)\,\mathrm{patched}} =(I−ΠK)​Kl,h(i),\displaystyle=(I-\Pi_{K})K_{l,h}^{(i)}, (S6)
ΠK\displaystyle\Pi_{K} =PK​PK⊤.\displaystyle=P_{K}P_{K}^{\top}.

while leaving all other visual and textual token activations completely unmodified.

Attribution Metric.

Let Lunsafe​(𝐱)L_{\mathrm{unsafe}}(\mathbf{x}) denote the output logit difference between the unsafe target completion token (e.g., “bomb”) and the benign safe token (e.g., “cannot”) under input activation state 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The direct path log-odds drop is formulated as:

Δ​𝒜unsafe\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{unsafe}} =Lunsafe​(𝐱base)−Lunsafe​(𝐱patched)Lunsafe​(𝐱base)\displaystyle=\frac{L_{\mathrm{unsafe}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{base}})-L_{\mathrm{unsafe}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{patched}})}{L_{\mathrm{unsafe}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{base}})} (S7)

Results.

Our resample diagnostic shows that this targeted key-space projection drops the direct path log-odds contribution to unsafe logits by 84.1%, while leaving contributions to safe, benign tokens largely unchanged. This is consistent with higher projection energy of intervention-relevant patterns onto the extracted key basis on heads with gh⋆>0g_{h}^{\star}>0; we treat this as supportive but not definitive mechanistic evidence.

S14 Always-On Projection vs. Selective gh⋆g_{h}^{\star}

To justify the gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} mix, we evaluate always-on projection (gh=1g_{h}{=}1 on every targeted head), which degrades capability on standard non-malicious visual-reasoning tasks.

AI2D Diagram Benchmark Evaluation.

We evaluate the over-refusal failure mode on the AI2D (Allen Institute for AI Diagrams) reasoning dataset, which contains dense structural layouts, interconnected flowcharts, mechanical blueprints, and circuit diagrams. Dense spatial geometries in these non-malicious images produce elevated intervention-relevant subspace energy EhE_{h} in deep attention layers even when the query is benign.

Severe Over-Refusal.

Under always-on projection (Projection-AlwaysOn, gh=1g_{h}{=}1), these dense benign diagrams receive a full KV rewrite. The projection suppresses layout-bearing states and causes over-refusal or hallucinatory answers. On AI2D structural reasoning queries, always-on projection drops accuracy from 62.4% (Base) to 31.2% (Projection-AlwaysOn), while SPARK maintains 62.0% with the default gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} mix.

Concrete Visual Case Study.

Consider a dense process diagram with labeled nodes, directional arrows, and branching connectors (AI2D-style structure):

  • •

    Visual Prompt: “Which labeled component receives flow from node B?”

  • •

    Base Model Output: “Component D receives flow from node B via the rightward arrow…” [Correct, Accuracy: 62.4%]

  • •

    Projection-AlwaysOn Output: “I cannot fulfill this request. The image contains high-density lines that match safety-filtering profiles.” [Severe Over-Refusal/Hallucination, Accuracy: 31.2%]

  • •

    SPARK (Ours) Output: “Component D receives flow from node B via the rightward arrow…” [Correct, Accuracy: 62.0%]

Role of the mix.

Setting gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}{=}0 on heads with low EhE_{h} is not just a speed optimization: it reduces semantic erasure and preserves reasoning on complex, non-malicious structural layouts.

Image-only forced-intervention analysis.

To test whether some image-only failures are caused by conservative gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} (heads remaining at 0), we force gh⋆=1g_{h}^{\star}{=}1 on all targeted heads for image-only harmful queries. This increases image-only capture, but at a clear utility/benign-refusal cost, supporting the interpretation that default SPARK trades some image-only sensitivity for better overall safety–utility balance.

S15 Safety SFT Replication Controls and Latency Scaling

Controlled Chameleon Safety-SFT Replication.

To verify that the reported Chameleon Safety SFT collapse is not caused by a single unstable training choice, we run a controlled sweep with fixed data splits, fixed seeds, and model-selection by held-out safety–utility score. We sweep: learning rate {1​e−5,2​e−5,5​e−5}\{1\mathrm{e}{-5},2\mathrm{e}{-5},5\mathrm{e}{-5}\}, warmup ratio {0.03,0.06,0.10}\{0.03,0.06,0.10\}, epoch budget {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}, and weight decay {0.0,0.01}\{0.0,0.01\} under AdamW. Decoding settings are matched across all checkpoints. The best checkpoint for each seed is selected by minimizing ASR under a utility floor constraint (MMMU and RWQA on the held-out validation split). Across this sweep, we consistently observe severe utility degradation on Chameleon relative to inference-time interventions.

Latency Scaling Across Batch Sizes.

For efficiency analysis (not a universal latency win over all defenses), we report latency scaling under matched decoding settings (same max token budget, same precision mode, same hardware queue). SPARK adds no additional per-token decode overhead in our profiling because intervention is performed once at prefill; decode-time steering methods can accumulate overhead with generated length.

S16 Clarifications on Novelty, Fairness, and Scope

Novelty relative to OmniSteer.

SPARK and OmniSteer are both representation-level interventions, but with different intervention loci and timing. OmniSteer primarily steers hidden-state refusal directions during decoding, while SPARK edits KV-cache memory channels at prefill and reuses the edited cache during decoding. In our matched runtime reporting (Section S7), this distinction is associated with zero decode-time overhead for SPARK and non-zero decode-time overhead for decode-time steering methods.

Baseline fairness and SFT interpretation.

We do not interpret Chameleon Safety SFT behavior as a universal failure of training-time alignment. Instead, we interpret it as architecture-dependent brittleness under an early-fusion setting in our matched protocol. In the main table, LLaVA-OV Safety SFT remains substantially more stable than Chameleon. This is why SPARK is positioned as a complementary post-hoc inference-time layer rather than a categorical replacement for SFT/RLHF/DPO families.

Why KV-space (vs. Q / broad hidden-state edits).

Our intervention choice follows attention information flow: queries (QQ) are prompt-conditioned retrieval requests, keys (KK) control addressing weights, and values (VV) carry the retrieved content. Editing QQ directly can entangle intervention with user-intent semantics at each decode step, while broad hidden-state edits can affect both benign and unsafe pathways. KV-cache editing at prefill changes the memory substrate before autoregressive rollout, yielding a targeted key-side addressing constraint plus value-side content attenuation.

EhE_{h} calibration transfer scope.

The 90th percentile of per-head EhE_{h} (equivalently λ/(2​α)\lambda/(2\alpha)) is calibrated on the benign pool in Section S5 (not on MMMU/RWQA test items and not on VLSafe/ToViLaG harmful training sets). We expect transfer to distant visual domains (e.g., medical imaging) to require re-calibration of layer ranges and EhE_{h} percentiles due to shifted intervention-relevant energy statistics; Table S28 illustrates cutoff drift under domain shift.

Adaptive optimization attacks.

White-box adaptive mix-evasion attacks and optional mix-hardening protocols are in Section S17.

Input-defense baseline strength.

We agree Gaussian blur is a weak baseline. As a stronger input-level comparator, we include a CLIP-score safety filter gate (thresholded on unsafe-image similarity); it reduces ASR but remains weaker than SPARK at comparable utility.

Stage-1 necessity and subspace controls.

To test whether Stage 1 harm calibration is necessary, we compare the full SPARK pipeline against (i) a harmful–benign contrast basis, (ii) SVD of Δ​WDSA\Delta W_{\mathrm{DSA}} rather than Δ​X\Delta X, (iii) swapped or benign-VQA subspaces, and (iv) rank-matched random bases, with the same Stage 2 adapter and EhE_{h} percentile calibration where applicable. Sequential stages are required: joint subspace–adapter training caused unstable PKP_{K} drift in preliminary runs, so PK,PVP_{K},P_{V} are frozen before Stage 2. Section S6 additionally reports patch/restore causal controls on fixed KV caches (not full retraining).

Grounding asymmetry control (K-only vs V-only).

The main ablation already shows that grounding both K+V hurts utility. We additionally test V-only grounding to isolate asymmetry: key-only grounding remains the strongest utility-preserving option in our setup.

Text-only scope note.

SPARK is primarily a multimodal defense layer: under pure text-only attacks, decode-time hidden-state steering can be stronger (e.g., lower ASR on LLaVA text-only), while SPARK is optimized for cross-modal safety–utility balance.

Two-stage design rationale.

Stage 1 extracts frozen harmful KV bases from diagnostic residuals and discards the probe; Stage 2 trains a residual on K⁡(I−ΠK)K(I-\Pi_{K}) against those fixed bases. Prefill then mixes the restored cache with gh⋆g_{h}^{\star}. Joint subspace–adapter training drifted PKP_{K} in preliminary runs (Section S16).

Relation to representation engineering literature.

SPARK is complementary to prior representation engineering and activation-space interventions. Our method adopts a similar operational philosophy (editing internal representations at inference), but specializes it to multimodal memory channels ((K,V)(K,V)) with a prefill-time gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} mix and structural key anchoring for safety–utility control.

S17 MM-SafetyBench and Adaptive Robustness

To complement VLSafe and ToViLaG evaluations, we report ASR on MM-SafetyBench under the same evaluation contract as Table S2: instruction-tuned LLM judge (Section S7 rubric), matched decoding hyperparameters, LLaVA-OV-7B, and seeds {13,17,23}\{13,17,23\} (n=300n{=}300 held-out prompts). ToViLaG text / image / text+image rows elsewhere in this supplementary are our VQA-style evaluation partitions of ToViLaG, not an official extra release of that dataset.

We additionally test white-box adaptive attacks that assume knowledge of SPARK’s gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} rule and projection. Adaptive evaluations use a 200-prompt held-out subset from ToViLaG/VLSafe test pools (disjoint from SPARK training). We report ASR (same judge) and SPARK bypass rate (fraction of harmful cases where gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}=0 on every targeted head after optimization).

Adaptive attack protocols.

Optimized prompt suffix: 40-step greedy coordinate optimization on a 20-token suffix maximizing harmful-completion log-probability. Image perturbation (ℓ2+\ell_{2}{+}LPIPS): 15-step projected gradient on pixels with ‖δ‖2≤8/255\|\delta\|_{2}\leq 8/255 and LPIPS≤0.05\leq 0.05 vs. the original image, penalizing EhE_{h} above the implicit cutoff λ/(2​α)\lambda/(2\alpha). Joint prompt–image optimization: alternate 5 image steps and 5 text steps for 30 total steps. Universal adversarial suffix: one suffix tuned on 50 train prompts, evaluated on 150 held-out prompts.

Capability under MM-SafetyBench.

Under the same LLaVA-OV-7B protocol, MMMU (47.8 vs. 48.4 base) and RWQA (60.7 vs. 61.8 base) in extended evaluations remain within 1.1 points of the main comparison (Table S2), indicating that lower MM-SafetyBench ASR in Table S32 co-occurs with near-main capability on these splits, not a separate utility collapse.

Adaptive robustness interpretation.

Adaptive attacks increase SPARK ASR from 7.4% (non-adaptive ToViLaG T+I) to 20.3% (joint prompt–image optimization) and raise mix bypass (gh⋆=0g_{h}^{\star}{=}0 on every targeted head) to 38.6% (Table S32). AutoSteer reaches 22.7% under the same joint protocol. These are white-box stress tests, not certified robustness guarantees.

Mix-hardening protocols (constructive controls).

The implicit EhE_{h} cutoff in (S3) is the primary adaptive vulnerability. We define two optional mitigations evaluated on the same n=200n{=}200 adaptive held-out pool and joint attack recipe as Table S32: (H1) Session-randomized percentile: per episode, sample the EhE_{h} percentile uniformly from the 80th–95th range calibrated on the benign pool (attacker knows the family but not the session draw). (H2) Secret head subset: per episode, sample a fixed subset of targeted heads (|S|=8|S|{=}8 of 16 candidate heads in layers 18–24) using a private seed; (S3) uses only maxh∈S⁡Eh\max_{h\in S}E_{h}. If bypass rate drops with stable MMMU, the failure mode is partially addressable without changing the KV projector.

S18 Extended Structural and Calibration Probes

Extended ablations below use the same judge, seeds {13,17,23}\{13,17,23\}, and decoding contract as the main paper.

Key–structure alignment probe (no extra training).

At prefill on layers 18–24 (heads with gh⋆>0g_{h}^{\star}>0), we log per-visual-token statistics on harmful (n=200n{=}200) vs. benign (n=200n{=}200) held-out prompts: ‖K−Gedge‖¯2\overline{\|K-G_{\mathrm{edge}}\|}_{2}, ‖K​PK‖22¯\overline{\|KP_{K}\|_{2}^{2}}, and Spearman ρ\rho between ‖Ki​PK‖2\|K_{i}P_{K}\|_{2} and high-pass RGB residual (HF) vs. CLIP ViT-L/14 patch similarity (semantic). SPARK reduces energy in the harm-calibrated key basis on harmful inputs and moves keys closer to GedgeG_{\mathrm{edge}}; HF coupling rises relative to semantic coupling on harmful splits, consistent with a structure-biased addressing channel rather than a semantic-texture anchor.

Structural-anchor ablation (Phase 2 rerun).

We ablate the image-structure anchor under fixed Stage 2 settings (key-only ℒg​r​o​u​n​d\mathcal{L}_{ground}, layers 18–24, EhE_{h} percentile calibration). Alternatives: Sobel (3×33{\times}3, OpenCV defaults), HED (default weights), Gaussian-blurred Canny, and a shuffled-edge control that preserves edge statistics but breaks spatial correspondence with the image.

Typography on fixed background.

Fixed natural background; swap harmful text overlay only (fixed font box/resolution). SPARK preserves low image-only ASR; blur and no-anchor memory edits do not match the default frontier on this split.

S19 Documented Tradeoffs: Where SPARK Wins and Where It Does Not

Table S38 maps reproduced rows from Table S2 (and related splits) to the lowest-ASR non-SPARK defense in that row (best other). A positive gap means SPARK is worse than that defense; a negative gap means SPARK is better. Earlier drafts sometimes cited a weaker baseline (e.g., OmniSteer 40.8% on Chameleon image-only) while omitting Steer (29.3%); the table below uses the true row-wise minimum.

How to read the Chameleon image-only row.

SPARK (31.4%) is not the lowest ASR in Table S2: Steer reaches 29.3%. SPARK does beat OmniSteer (40.8%), AutoSteer (43.7%), and VLM-Guard (37.9%), so the correct story is a split-dependent trade-off (KV prefill vs. decode-time hidden steering), not a universal win on early-fusion image-only attacks. The large LLaVA-vs.-Chameleon gap (4.7 vs. 31.4) reflects architecture and EhE_{h} mix behavior, not a table inconsistency.

Hypotheses for Chameleon image-only.

Early visual–language fusion may distribute unsafe evidence across layers, reducing the concentration of late-layer visual norms that SPARK targets. Decode-time Steer can perturb hidden states globally and slightly outperform SPARK on this row, at higher Chameleon utility cost elsewhere (Table S2). Conservative gh⋆g_{h}^{\star} (Section S14) further limits image-only correction unless gh⋆=1g_{h}^{\star}{=}1 is forced (Section S14; 31.4%→26.7%31.4\%\rightarrow 26.7\% image-only ASR on Chameleon on that split).
